title: Rupee and Paise Board
context: Grade 4, the first working topic of the money chapter, built on the recap exercise that opens it. An adult sees rupees turned into paise, which looks like Class 3 revision. What is actually being settled is the one fact that every later topic with paise in it leans on: a hundred paise make one rupee. The chapter never states it, though its recap cannot be done without it and its first subtraction example breaks a rupee by it. Paise here are an amount on a price tag and never a coin, so the tool shows them as cells of a rupee strip and not as small change.

writeup.why: Break a rupee into a hundred paise, read the dot on a price tag, write any amount in paise alone, and compare two amounts once both are in paise.
writeup.look: A rupee tray and a paise tray side by side under a price tag, a paise meter below them, and two tags with a sign slot between them at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Rupee and Paise Board' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the strips filled against the rupees the tray began with on the first phase, and on the others the tags built, matched or compared against the tags this phase lays out, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each strip fills or each tag settles, and the second fixed at what this phase holds. On the first phase the trade control stays unlit, so the count there only climbs. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The price tag runs across the top of the working area, 714 by 88 at 64,214: Rs in ink, then the rupees in deep blue, the vermilion dot, and two boxes after it for the paise in green, both boxes drawn on every tag so that the two places are seen before either is filled. The rupee tray stands under it at the left, 290 by 300 at 64,318, holding play rupee coins in rows of ten with any play notes above them, each piece showing only its value in large figures. The paise tray stands to its right, 352 by 300 at 426,318, holding rupee strips one under another, each 332 by 32 and ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, with a heavier near-black rule between the blocks. It shows up to seven strips at full length, and each full strip past seven joins a neat stack at its foot with the number of strips written beside it in sky blue. Between the two trays stand the break control, a curved arrow 56 by 56 at 362,392, and the trade control under it at 362,480. Break lifts one rupee coin out of the rupee tray, carries it across and opens it into a full strip, its cells filling block by block from the left; trade folds a full strip back up into one coin and carries it home. The paise meter runs under both trays, 714 by 64 at 64,634, reading in green every paise in the paise tray. It climbs by a hundred as a strip fills and drops by a hundred as one is traded, and a flap can be drawn down over it while it goes on counting behind. On the third phase, lifting the flap first opens every rupee still in the rupee tray into its strip, in one sweep from left to right, so what the meter then shows is the whole amount in paise. At the right of the working area stand the two compared tags, each 150 by 88, at 790,318 and 1000,318, with the sign slot, 50 by 88, between them at 945,318, and the same-unit switch under all three, 360 by 56 at 790,430. The switch rewrites a tag in rupees as the same amount in paise, its rupees multiplied by a hundred and its paise added, and leaves a tag already in paise as it was; the sign slot opens only while both tags are in the same unit, both written with Rs or both in paise alone. On the third phase the same right-hand place holds one card written as a sum of smaller amounts above three price tags, and a matched pair is joined by a near-black line. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across on every phase, with a unit tag under the slot reading rupees or paise, whichever the question asks for, filled in beside the number and never left off. On the second phase a dot key stands beside the twelve, and the slot becomes a small price tag of its own with both paise boxes drawn. On the fourth phase three keys sit over the pad reading greater than, less than and equals. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own and are the pictures' colours too. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue. The paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion, a clear round dot, and wherever amounts stand in columns it sits on a near-black dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count of things is not money. The zeros that fill the paise column of a whole-rupee amount in column working are grey. Every play note is one plain pale blue rectangle and every play coin one plain steel disc, all notes one size and all coins one size, each printed with its value and nothing else. No coin below one rupee is drawn anywhere: paise are shaded cells on a strip ruled into a hundred in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome: every column rule, dotted line, tick, bracket, strike line, bill rule and panel edge is near-black. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in, a count by the box beside the times sign or the slot marked things, and the change or money left by the tray or line that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour. Grey never means faint: a zero in a paise column is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through once with the new figure written above it, and never rubbed out. A full strip is one rupee and a part-shaded strip is less than one rupee, so no strip on this stage holds more than a hundred cells. Nothing standing for paise is round, and both paise boxes are drawn on every tag, filled or not, so a small number of paise is never seen with its first place missing.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last amount the child built, its price tag and its paise meter, and the two tags they compared with the sign between them.

phases.win: each strip fills with a hundred cells, and the meter climbs by exactly one hundred every time
phases.does: breaks one rupee into a full strip of cells, watches the meter climb, breaks the rest, then says how many paise the rupees made
phases.goal: a hundred paise make one rupee, so rupees become paise when multiplied by a hundred
phases.says: Break one rupee. How many paise does it make?
phases.check: Away from the screen: how many paise are there in eight rupees? And in eighty rupees?
phases.feels: every rupee opens into the same long strip, and the meter jumps a whole hundred for each one
phases.hands: Hand round play rupee coins and a sheet of paper strips, each ruled into a hundred cells in ten blocks of ten. Say it first, in these words: a hundred paise make one rupee. Swap one coin for one strip and count the strip in tens with the class, ten, twenty, all the way to a hundred. Then put five coins on a desk and ask how many paise they would make if every one were swapped.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many cells are on one strip? Second rung, the phase's: how far did the meter climb when one rupee opened? Third rung: the tray is cut to one coin, and the child opens it and counts its strip in blocks of ten before the larger amount comes back. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: counting in tens is a habit that place-value lessons build, and a strip drawn in ten blocks looks like ten of something.
wrong.move: writes three hundred and sixty paise for Rs 36, as if ten paise made a rupee.
wrong.screen: the break control opens the first of the thirty-six coins at walking pace, its strip filling block by block, and the meter climbs by one hundred, not by ten. Two more coins open the same way, and the child's three hundred and sixty is shown on the meter's scale: it falls sixty past the third hundred, three rupees and sixty paise, with thirty-three coins still waiting in the tray. The child's number stays in the slot, nothing marked.

wrong.why: changing the unit sounds like changing the name of the amount, not its number, and thirty-six is the only number in the question.
wrong.move: answers thirty-six, the number the question began with, and writes it as paise.
wrong.screen: thirty-six cells are shaded on one strip in the paise tray, less than half of it, beside the thirty-six coins still standing in their rows. One coin is then opened beside them, and its strip alone runs far past all thirty-six cells. The unit tag under the slot lights paise, and the child's thirty-six stays written in it.

phases.screen: a few rupee coins in the rupee tray, an empty paise tray, and the paise meter reading nothing
phases.soWhat: A hundred paise make one rupee, so rupees become paise when multiplied by a hundred.
phases.concept: A hundred paise make a rupee

phases.win: the trays match the tag, and a small number of paise settles with a zero in the first place after the dot
phases.does: builds the tag's amount, rupees into the rupee tray and shaded cells into the paise tray, then writes a tag for fewer than ten paise
phases.goal: in an amount written with a dot, rupees come before the dot and the paise take the two places after it
phases.says: Which part of the tag is rupees? How many places do the paise take?
phases.check: Write seventeen rupees and five paise with a dot. How many places did the paise take?
phases.feels: the two places after the dot hold one number of paise between them, and a small one needs a zero in front
phases.hands: Write Rs 30.45 on the board and cover everything after the dot. Ask what the uncovered part is, then uncover the two places and ask what they are together. Then ask the class to write seventeen rupees and five paise with a dot, and let two children who write it differently each shade their paise on a strip, so the class sees which one shows five cells.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which part of the tag is rupees? Second rung, the phase's: how many places do the paise take? Third rung: the tag is cut to one rupee and a few paise, and the child shades the cells and watches both boxes fill before the larger tag comes back. The number pad and the dot key stay open.

wrong.why: a digit standing on its own looks like a number on its own, and the first one after the dot is the one the eye meets.
wrong.move: reads Rs 40.25 as forty rupees and two paise, taking only the first place after the dot as the paise.
wrong.screen: the trays build the child's reading, forty rupees in the rupee tray and two cells shaded on a strip, and the tag it makes is written beside the question as Rs 40.02, with a zero in the first place. The two boxes of the question's tag then light together as one number, twenty-five, and twenty-five cells shade. Both readings stay built side by side, nothing marked.

wrong.why: four digits in a row are read as one number everywhere else, and a small dot is easy to step over.
wrong.move: reads Rs 40.25 as four thousand and twenty-five rupees, reading straight past the dot.
wrong.screen: the dot on the tag glows vermilion and the digits part at it: the forty before it goes to the rupee tray as forty coins and the twenty-five after it to the paise tray as twenty-five cells. The break control then opens the forty coins one after another, and the meter climbs to four thousand and twenty-five paise: the child's digits, but a number of paise, a hundred times less than four thousand and twenty-five rupees. The child's reading stays in the slot.

wrong.why: eight paise is one digit, and one digit seems to need only one place.
wrong.move: writes sixty-four rupees and eight paise as Rs 64.8, leaving the second place after the dot empty.
wrong.screen: the tag keeps both paise boxes drawn, and with the eight in the first box and the second left open, the strip shades eighty cells, which is what Rs 64.8 would say. A zero is then set in the first box and the eight moves to the second, and the shading falls back to eight cells. Both tags stand side by side, and the child's is still written in the slot.

phases.screen: a price tag with a dot in it, and the two trays empty
phases.soWhat: Rupees come before the dot and the paise take the two places after it, so eight paise are written 08.
phases.concept: The dot between rupees and paise

phases.win: the meter uncovers on the child's number, and each matched pair of tags is joined
phases.does: says how many paise the rupees make, adds the paise on the strip, then uncovers the meter, and matches amounts written as sums to the same amounts written with a dot
phases.goal: an amount is written in paise alone by turning the rupees into hundreds of paise and adding the paise
phases.says: How many paise do the rupees make? Now add the paise on the strip.
phases.check: Write Rs 26.05 in paise alone. Then write Rs 20 and Rs 6 and 5 paise the same way.
phases.feels: the rupees turn into hundreds, and the paise just join on at the end
phases.hands: Lay three rupee coins and a strip with forty-five cells shaded on a desk. Ask how many paise the coins would make if each were swapped for a strip, and write that. Then count the shaded cells and add them on. Last, write the same money as Rs 3.45 and as a sum, Rs 2 and Rs 1 and 45 paise, and ask whether any of the three ways is more money than the others.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many paise do the rupees make? Second rung, the phase's: how many paise are on the strip? Third rung: the board is cut to one rupee coin and a strip with a few cells shaded, and the child writes that in paise before the larger amount comes back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: there are two numbers on the tag, and adding them is the quickest thing to do with two numbers.
wrong.move: adds fifty-three and forty and writes ninety-three paise for Rs 53.40.
wrong.screen: the flap lifts and every coin opens into its strip in one sweep, fifty-three strips and forty cells more, and the meter climbs past five thousand and stops at five thousand three hundred and forty. The child's ninety-three is shaded as ninety-three cells on one strip beside the stack, less than a single rupee, and stays in the slot.

wrong.why: the digits five, three and four look finished once they are all written, and a zero at the end looks like nothing.
wrong.move: drops the last zero and writes five hundred and thirty-four paise.
wrong.screen: the child's five hundred and thirty-four is built in the trays beside the question's amount: five strips and thirty-four cells, five rupees and thirty-four paise, set against fifty-three rupees and forty paise. The meter reads the two amounts one after the other, and the child's number stays in the slot.

phases.screen: a filled board, some rupees and one part-shaded strip, with the paise meter covered
phases.soWhat: An amount is written in paise alone by turning the rupees into hundreds of paise and adding the paise.

phases.win: both tags show paise, and the sign drops into the slot the right way round
phases.does: flips the same-unit switch to write both tags in paise, compares the two numbers, and sets the sign
phases.goal: two amounts are compared once both are in the same unit, and equal amounts take the equals sign
phases.says: One tag is in rupees and one is in paise. Can you compare them yet?
phases.check: Which is more, Rs 38 or 3850 paise? Say what you turned into what before you chose.
phases.feels: the sign cannot be chosen until both amounts count the same thing
phases.hands: Write sixty rupees on one card and six thousand one hundred paise on another, and ask which is more. Let the class argue, then turn the sixty rupees into paise together, six thousand, before anyone sets a sign. Then write Rs 45 and Rs 35 on one card and eight thousand paise on another, and ask which sign goes between them.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what unit is each tag in? Second rung, the phase's: how many paise is the rupee tag? Third rung: the tags are cut to one rupee against ninety paise, and the child turns the rupee into paise before the larger pair comes back. The sign keys and the number pad stay open.

wrong.why: the rupee is the bigger unit, so any number of rupees feels bigger than any number of paise.
wrong.move: sets greater than after ninety rupees, against nine thousand two hundred and thirty paise, because rupees are worth more than paise.
wrong.screen: the sign slot stays shut, and the child's sign waits beside it. The same-unit switch then rewrites ninety rupees as nine thousand paise, and the two tags stand in one unit, nine thousand against nine thousand two hundred and thirty. The slot opens with the child's sign still waiting beside it, nothing marked.

wrong.why: six thousand nine hundred and fifty has far more digits than seventy, and for two plain numbers the one with more digits is the bigger.
wrong.move: compares the bare numbers seventy and six thousand nine hundred and fifty, and decides the paise amount is bigger.
wrong.screen: the slot stays shut and the switch rewrites seventy rupees as seven thousand paise, which stands above six thousand nine hundred and fifty. The same habit of comparing by the digits gives the right sign for ninety rupees against nine thousand two hundred and thirty paise, and both pairs are then set side by side in paise to show that it was luck there. The child's sign stays beside the slot.

phases.screen: two tags side by side, one in rupees and one in paise alone, with the sign slot empty
phases.soWhat: Put both amounts in the same unit before comparing them. When both come to the same number of paise, the equals sign goes between them.

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the flap is lifted. Every rupee still in the rupee tray lifts in turn, left to right, crosses the gap and opens into its strip, the strips stacking in the paise tray while the meter races up a hundred at a time; the part-shaded strip is counted last, cell by cell, and the meter stops on one number and holds. The child's own number stands in the slot beside it the whole time. Dropping the flap sends the coins home again, and it can be lifted and dropped as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the rupee coins of the question stand in rows of ten in the rupee tray, the paise tray is empty and the paise meter reads nothing. On the second a price tag with a dot in it stands above two empty trays, both of its paise boxes drawn. On the third the trays are already filled, some rupees on the left and one part-shaded strip on the right, with the flap drawn down over the paise meter. On the fourth two tags stand side by side at the right, one in rupees and one in paise alone, with the sign slot shut and the same-unit switch off. The running count at the top left holds the strips filled or the tags settled against what this phase lays out, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: a rupee coin, or the dot on the tag, or the flap over the meter, or the same-unit switch, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what one rupee is made of. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any amount built in the trays, with the break control, the paise meter and the sign slot open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the paise in a rupee, reading and writing the dot, amounts in paise alone, and comparing two amounts in the same unit.
voiceLines: Rupees on one side and paise on the other. What is one rupee made of?
Break one rupee. How many paise does it make?
Which part of the tag is rupees? How many places do the paise take?
How many paise do the rupees make? Now add the paise on the strip.
One tag is in rupees and one is in paise. Can you compare them yet?
A new amount. Read the tag before you touch the trays.
Free play. Any amount, with the break, the meter and the sign slot open.
Open one rupee again, and watch how far the meter climbs.
Every rupee opened into its hundred, every tag read, and every pair compared in one unit.

observations.why: Each rupee opens into one full strip, and a full strip holds a hundred cells.
observations.soWhat: A hundred paise make one rupee, so rupees become paise when multiplied by a hundred.
observations.observe: The meter climbed by exactly one hundred each time a rupee was opened.

observations.why: The two places after the dot hold one number of paise between them, and eight is too small to reach the first place.
observations.soWhat: Rupees come before the dot and the paise take the two places after it, so eight paise are written 08.
observations.observe: Every tag had two paise boxes, and eight paise filled the first one with a zero.

observations.why: Every rupee opened into a hundred cells, and the shaded cells on the part strip were counted after them.
observations.soWhat: An amount is written in paise alone by turning the rupees into hundreds of paise and adding the paise.
observations.observe: When the flap lifted, the meter stopped on a hundred for every rupee with the strip's paise added on.

observations.why: A number of rupees and a number of paise count different things, so the bare numbers cannot be set against each other.
observations.soWhat: Put both amounts in the same unit before comparing them, and equal amounts take the equals sign.
observations.observe: The sign slot stayed shut until both tags were in the same unit.

source_tool.blurb: See that a hundred paise make one rupee, read the dot that separates rupees from paise, write an amount in paise alone, and compare two amounts once both are in the same unit.

serves.exercise: matching five amounts in rupees and paise with the same amounts written another way
putting greater than, less than or equals between six pairs of amounts

source_tool.description: A money board fills the stage with a rupee tray on the left, a paise tray on the right and a price tag above them. Rupees are drawn as notes and coins, each showing only its value. Paise are never drawn as coins. They are cells on a rupee strip, a strip ruled into a hundred equal cells, so a full strip is exactly one rupee and a part-shaded strip shows the paise. A break control lifts one rupee out of the rupee tray and opens it in the paise tray as a full strip of a hundred cells, and a full strip in the paise tray trades back for one rupee. A paise meter under the trays counts the paise in the paise tray, which is the whole amount in paise once every rupee is opened into its strip, and it can be covered while the child works the number out. The price tag writes the amount with the rupees before the dot and the paise in the two places after it, so fewer than ten paise fill the first place with a zero. On the right, two price tags stand side by side with a sign slot between them for greater than, less than or equals, and a same-unit switch writes both tags in paise; the slot takes a sign only once both tags are in the same unit.
source_tool.art_direction: A rupee opened into a hundred cells / Picture book

wrong.note: A soft low double-bloop. A nudge, never a buzzer.

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a rupee tray and a paise tray, strips ruled into a hundred cells, a counting tray of value slots, a bill slip with a dotted line, a shop counter with a change tray, a multiplying frame under a row of things, and a till with a share mat.

Every note and coin shows its value in large figures and nothing else: no design, no picture, no lettering but the value. Every note is a plain paper rectangle and every coin a plain metal disc, all notes one size and one colour and all coins one size and one metal, so a value is read from its print and never from size or colour.

No coin below one rupee is drawn or named anywhere. Wherever paise are drawn rather than written, they are shaded cells on a rupee strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is exactly one rupee. Nothing standing for paise is ever round.

Written money with paise is Rs, the rupees, a dot and two digits of paise, as Rs 96.75. Fewer than ten paise are written with a zero in the first place after the dot. A whole amount in running text is written with no dot, as Rs 43.

Column working always stands on a dotted line: every dot in a column sits on it, rupees to its left and paise to its right. In column working a whole-rupee amount carries two zeros in its paise column, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit.

A hundred paise rolling up into one rupee is always shown moving, from the paise column into a small carry circle over the rupees, and a rupee broken into paise is always shown opening into a full strip of a hundred cells.
A rupees figure that goes down by one is struck through and the new figure written above it, never erased, so the break can be read afterwards.
The number of things in a product is a count. It stands in a box of its own beside the times sign, outside the rupees and paise columns, with no dot, and no cell exists for it under the paise.
Every answer slot carries its unit, rupees or things, printed beside the number.
A total, a change, a cost or an amount left is told apart by the slot or line it sits in first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a note, a coin, a cell or a slot the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The rupees of every amount, the rupees column and the value printed on every note and coin are deep blue, and the paise of every amount, the paise column and every cell standing for paise are green. The dot between rupees and paise is vermilion in every tool, drawn as a clear round dot on the dotted line. A rupee carried from the paise, and a rupee broken into a hundred paise with the digits it rewrites, are amber. The change handed back, the money left and a remainder are reddish purple, so money coming back is never mistaken for a cost. A count of things, a number multiplied by, how many notes of one value or how many can be bought, is sky blue, because a count is never money. The two zeros in the paise column of a whole-rupee amount are grey, drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and never faded. Every play note is one plain pale blue and every play coin one plain steel, so a value is read from its print and never from its colour. All of that holds in greyscale, because a digit is told apart by the column it stands in, a carry by the circle it sits in and a count by the box beside the times sign, before any of them is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Open one rupee again, and watch how far the meter climbs.
voice.onNext: A new amount. Read the tag before you touch the trays.
voice.opening: Rupees on one side and paise on the other. What is one rupee made of?
voice.onFinish: Every rupee opened into its hundred, every tag read, and every pair compared in one unit.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any amount, with the break, the meter and the sign slot open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A hundred paise make a rupee
The dot between rupees and paise

placement.where: After play rupee coins and a sheet of paper strips ruled into a hundred cells have been handed round, and a coin has been swapped for a full strip by hand. The tool is what keeps the paise meter and the price tag moving together while a rupee is broken, which a coin and a strip on a desk cannot show.

answer_key.rule: A hundred paise make one rupee, so an amount in rupees becomes paise when it is multiplied by a hundred, and every full hundred paise is one rupee. In an amount written with a dot, the rupees come before the dot and the paise take the two places after it, so eight paise are written with a zero before the eight. An amount in rupees and paise is written in paise alone by turning the rupees into hundreds of paise and adding the paise. An amount made up of several smaller amounts is worth their sum. Two amounts are compared once both are in the same unit, and when both come to the same number of paise they are equal and the equals sign goes between them.
answer_key.wrong: The rupee in question is broken again at walking pace, the paise meter climbing by a hundred as the strip fills, and the two places after the dot are lit in turn. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: A hundred paise make one rupee.
So each of the 36 rupees is 100 paise, and 36 rupees are 36 times 100 paise.
36 times 100 is 3600, so Rs 36 is 3600 paise.
items.question: A shopkeeper counts Rs 36 in rupee coins. How many paise is that?
items.checkpoint: A hundred paise make one rupee, so rupees become paise when multiplied by a hundred.
items.misconception: Writing 360 paise, as if ten paise made a rupee, or leaving the answer as 36.

steps: The dot separates the rupees from the paise.
The 64 before the dot is rupees.
The paise take the two places after the dot, so 08 is 8 paise.
items.question: A price tag reads Rs 64.08. How many rupees and how many paise is that?
items.checkpoint: Rupees come before the dot, and the paise take the two places after it.
items.misconception: Reading 08 as 80 paise, or writing 64 rupees and 8 paise as Rs 64.8, which reads as 80 paise.

steps: 53 rupees are 53 times 100 paise, which is 5300 paise.
The 40 after the dot is 40 paise more.
5300 and 40 make 5340, so Rs 53.40 is 5340 paise.
items.question: Write Rs 53.40 in paise alone.
items.checkpoint: To write an amount in paise alone, turn the rupees into hundreds of paise and add the paise.
items.misconception: Adding 53 and 40 to get 93 paise, or dropping the last zero and writing 534 paise.

steps: One amount is in rupees and the other in paise, so put both in paise first.
Rs 70 is 70 times 100 paise, which is 7000 paise.
7000 paise is more than 6950 paise, so Rs 70 > 6950 paise.
items.answer: Rs 70 is greater than 6950 paise, because Rs 70 is 7000 paise
items.question: Put greater than, less than or equals between Rs 70 and 6950 paise.
items.checkpoint: Put both amounts in the same unit before comparing them.
items.misconception: Comparing the bare numbers 70 and 6950 and deciding that the paise amount is bigger.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: How many paise make Rs 15?
items.final_answer: 1500 paise, because each rupee is 100 paise

items.question: A jar holds 900 paise. How many rupees is that?
items.final_answer: Rs 9, because every 100 paise make one rupee

items.question: Write 27 rupees and 45 paise with a dot.
Write 12 rupees and 6 paise with a dot.
items.final_answer: Rs 12.06. The paise take two places after the dot, so 6 paise is written 06

items.question: Write Rs 48.60 in paise alone.
items.final_answer: 4860 paise. 48 rupees are 4800 paise, and 60 more make 4860

items.question: Which of these matches Rs 50 + Rs 10 + Rs 2 + 30 paise: Rs 62.30, Rs 60.32 or 6203 paise?
items.final_answer: Rs 62.30. The rupees add to 62 and the paise are 30. 6203 paise is Rs 62.03

items.question: Put greater than, less than or equals between Rs 30 + Rs 45 and 7500 paise.
items.final_answer: Equals. Rs 30 and Rs 45 make Rs 75, which is 7500 paise

items.question: Which is more, Rs 84.50 or 8405 paise?
items.final_answer: Rs 84.50, because it is 8450 paise, and 8450 is more than 8405

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds rupees as notes and coins, each showing only its value
holds paise as shaded cells on rupee strips of a hundred cells each
opens one rupee into a full strip of a hundred paise
turns a full strip of a hundred paise back into one rupee
writes the amount with rupees before the dot and paise in two places after it
counts the paise in the paise tray, the whole amount once every rupee is opened, and can be covered
writes both compared tags in paise
takes greater than, less than or equals between two tags in the same unit

teaching_notes: Hand round play rupee coins and a sheet of paper strips ruled into a hundred cells before the tool is opened, and swap a coin for a full strip by hand. Say the fact first, in these words: a hundred paise make one rupee. The chapter never states it, yet its recap cannot be done without it and its first subtraction example breaks a rupee by it. It is Class 3 knowledge, and every later topic with paise in it uses it. Paise are an amount on a price tag, not a coin in a purse, so no small coin appears here, only cells on a strip. When a tag has fewer than ten paise, the first place after the dot holds a zero, because the paise always take two places. The recap's comparing question sets two pairs whose amounts come out the same, and there the equals sign is the answer. Put both amounts into paise before any sign is chosen.
generation_prompt: Build a money board on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A rupee tray sits on the left of the working area and a paise tray on the right, under a price tag. Rupees are drawn as notes and coins, each showing only its value in large figures. Paise are never drawn as coins: they are shaded cells on a rupee strip, a strip ruled into a hundred equal cells in ten blocks of ten, so a full strip is one rupee. A break control lifts one rupee from the rupee tray and opens it in the paise tray as a full strip, and a full strip can be traded back for one rupee. A paise meter under the trays counts the paise in the paise tray, which is the whole amount once every rupee is opened, and can be covered. The price tag writes the amount with the rupees before the dot and the paise in exactly two places after it, filling the first place with a zero for fewer than ten paise. At the right, two price tags stand side by side with a sign slot between them for greater than, less than or equals; a same-unit switch rewrites both in paise, and the slot takes a sign only once both tags are in the same unit. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Break a rupee into a hundred paise. Read the tag: rupees before the dot, paise after it. Turn rupees into paise to write an amount in paise. Put both amounts in paise before you compare.
